title: FlashReFocus: Interactive Image Refocusing in Seconds

paper.title: FlashReFocus: Interactive Image Refocusing in Seconds
paper.abstract: Abstract Single-image refocusing changes the focal plane and depth of field of a photograph after capture. It is inherently interactive: users try many focal points and blur strengths on one image, so each edit should be fast and change only the blur. Recent generative methods, however, rerun large diffusion models for every edit. We observe that the two sub-problems differ in kind: recovering the all-in-focus image is ill-posed and needs a generative prior, whereas rendering blur is largely determined by depth and the focal plane. We therefore propose FlashReFocus, which runs diffusion once per photograph and renders every edit with a lightweight network. To address the ill-posed restoration, a one-step diffusion deblurrer with a decoder refiner recovers fine detail efficiently while balancing fidelity and perceptual quality. For precise control, the renderer is conditioned on an explicit defocus map and uses defocus-bias attention, which lets pixels at similar defocus share information without interference from pixels at other depths; in-focus content stays unchanged, and editing the map yields tilt-shift and two focal planes. To further test generalization to unseen cameras, we collect 3CReal, a three-camera benchmark of 89 pairs. FlashReFocus achieves the best perceptual fidelity for zero-shot bokeh rendering on EBB! and 3CReal, refocuses 148.3 × 148.3\times faster than GenRefocus, and takes about half a second per further edit, 462 × 462\times faster.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Figure 1 : Refocusing paradigms. (a) Single-stage diffusion and (b) two-stage generative refocusing run a large diffusion model for every focal edit. (c) FlashReFocus restores the AiF image once and renders each new focal setting with a 1.3M-parameter network. (d) Seconds at 1536 × 1536 1536\times 1536 for deblurring, the first edit, each next edit, and both edits together. Figure 2 : Overview of FlashReFocus. (A) Stage I restores an all-in-focus image 𝐈 ^ AiF \hat{\mathbf{I}}_{\text{AiF}} in one step with a frozen latent diffusion U-Net and an optional decoder refiner; (B) ω \omega mixes the pixel and detail LoRA passes to trade fidelity for detail. (C) Stage II computes a defocus map from monocular depth and the selected focal point, and (D) renders bokeh in a single feed-forward pass with (E) defocus-bias attention, which focuses attention on tokens of similar defocus, more sharply for a larger strength K K . The bottom row shows the training phases. Depth of field determines which parts of a photograph appear sharp and is fixed at capture. Smartphone portrait modes move the focus afterwards only by blurring an already sharp image with depth recorded at capture [ 61 ] , so out-of-focus content stays blurred. Single-image refocusing lifts this limit by recovering an all-in-focus (AiF) image and re-rendering blur around a new focal plane [ 41 ] . Refocusing is interactive: a user tries several focal points and blur strengths on one photograph. Its two sub-problems differ in kind. Defocus is many-to-one: it discards high frequencies, so recovering the AiF image is ill-posed and needs a learned prior; regression-based restorers [ 25 , 73 ] over-smooth it [ 7 ] , whereas diffusion priors [ 18 , 46 ] synthesize realistic detail. In contrast, rendering blur is nearly well-posed: given depth and a focal plane, the circle of confusion (CoC) largely fixes the blur [ 41 ] , so generation adds cost and error rather than information. Recent methods nevertheless use large diffusion models for both. DiffCamera [ 64 ] and MagicBokeh [ 54 ] map the input directly to the refocused image and leave no reusable AiF image; GenRefocus [ 36 ] and AnyBokeh [ 19 ] split the task but render with a second large diffusion model. Either way, every edit is a full generative pass that takes minutes at 1536 × 1536 1536\times 1536 and regenerates regions meant to stay sharp (Fig. 1 ). This asymmetry suggests three principles for interactive refocusing, all followed by FlashReFocus (Fig. 2 ). (i) Generate once, render many. A session of N N edits costs C restore + N ​ C render C_{\text{restore}}+N\,C_{\text{render}} , so the generative step belongs outside the editing loop: Stage I restores the AiF image once with one-step diffusion [ 57 ] , and each edit runs only a 1.3M-parameter renderer. (ii) Edit only the blur. Changing the focus should leave in-focus content untouched, so Stage II adds a residual to the fixed AiF image; across edits, in-focus regions stay at 44.4 dB PSNR against 29.0 dB for GenRefocus. (iii) Control through optics. The renderer is conditioned on an explicit defocus map whose product with the strength mirrors the CoC, so the strength acts as an aperture and editing the map yields effects beyond a single lens, such as tilt-shift and two focal planes. Concretely, Stage I blends a pixel-fidelity and a detail LoRA with one weight ω \omega to trade fidelity for detail, learns from mixed real and synthetic blur, and adds a decoder refiner that keeps text and edges VAE decoding distorts; Stage II’s defocus-bias attention lets pixels at similar defocus share information, so blur changes sharply at depth boundaries without interference from unrelated, possibly salient pixels at other depths. The costly prior thus runs once, where detail must be invented, and each edit runs a small network on a task that optics constrain, which makes FlashReFocus both fast and accurate. Rendering also needs data with diverse focal settings: real pairs [ 22 , 50 ] capture lens-specific bokeh at few focal planes, and synthetic pairs [ 38 ] any focal plane with simplified optics, so we pre-train on synthetic multi-focal scenes and adapt to real pairs. Both are single-camera datasets, so we introduce 3CReal, 89 pairs from three unseen cameras, to test cross-camera generalization. Our contributions are: • For interactive refocusing, we propose a restore-once, render-many framework: diffusion runs once per photograph, and each edit runs only a lightweight renderer at interactive speed, leaving in-focus content unchanged. • To address the ill-posedness of defocus deblurring, we adapt one-step diffusion with a VAE-decoder refiner, which recovers detail efficiently while balancing fidelity and perceptual quality in a simple, unified design. • For precise control without complex designs, we craft the renderer’s defocus-bias attention and explicit defocus map, which set focus, strength, and depth edits directly. • To further test generalization to unseen cameras, we collect 3CReal; on it and EBB!, FlashReFocus leads in perceptual fidelity, far faster than generative rivals.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Figure 3 : Stage I deblurs in one step with separate fidelity and detail LoRAs. (A) A frozen U-Net with both LoRAs restores the input latent. (B) The pixel LoRA, a VAE-encoder LoRA, and the input convolution are trained with ℒ pixel \mathcal{L}_{\text{pixel}} and then frozen while the detail LoRA is trained with LPIPS and CSD. (C) At inference, ω \omega weights the detail branch and the refiner decodes 𝐈 ^ AiF \hat{\mathbf{I}}_{\text{AiF}} . Image restoration and defocus deblurring. Convolutional and Transformer restorers optimize reconstruction losses [ 10 , 30 , 73 ] and achieve high PSNR and SSIM, yet the perception–distortion trade-off [ 7 ] motivates generative priors for perceptual quality. Unlike motion or uniform blur, defocus blur has a point-spread function that varies with scene depth and focal distance [ 74 , 6 ] . Classical methods estimate a spatially varying kernel and deconvolve [ 26 , 79 , 76 ] , while learned models predict kernels or adaptive filters or exploit dual-pixel cues [ 56 , 42 , 25 , 1 , 2 ] , train on light-field pairs [ 48 ] , or model image formation explicitly [ 77 ] . More recently, diffusion models provide a learned prior over natural images for ill-posed inverse problems [ 18 , 46 ] . Restoration methods condition on the degraded image, predict residuals, or fuse latent priors [ 69 , 33 , 13 ] , and recent defocus methods combine diffusion with Transformer features or fidelity-aware guidance [ 29 , 9 , 27 , 28 ] . However, diffusion priors can hallucinate texture [ 4 ] and VAE compression loses fine structures; these issues motivate our detail LoRA and decoder refiner. Bokeh rendering and refocusing. Classical renderers convolve depth-dependent kernels, trace rays, or scatter in image space [ 41 , 24 , 40 , 70 ] , and layered or light-field inputs add scene information [ 61 , 37 ] . Learned renderers instead fit camera-specific appearance from data: they predict depth from one image [ 63 ] , learn DSLR blur from EBB! pairs [ 22 ] , refine analytical scattering [ 38 ] , render inpainted multiplane images [ 39 ] , add a strength control [ 50 ] , or model occlusion [ 52 ] . More recently, BokehDiff, MagicBokeh, and DiffCamera bring diffusion to bokeh synthesis [ 78 , 54 , 64 ] , including depth-free rendering [ 53 ] , and Any-to-Bokeh extends one-step diffusion bokeh to video with multiplane conditioning [ 71 ] , while Bokeh Diffusion controls the blur level of text-to-image generation but not the focal plane [ 15 ] . Across these methods, control signals range from scalar strength to masks, depth maps, and multiplane images; in contrast, ours is a depth-derived signed defocus map with a global strength. Refocusing further combines restoration with rendering. RefocusGAN estimates an AiF radiance image before applying focal blur [ 49 ] ; DC 2 uses a dual-camera rig [ 5 ] ; and GenRefocus trains two diffusion transformers, DeblurNet and BokehNet, for the two operations with semi-supervised learning [ 36 ] . Other methods avoid an explicit AiF image: Learning to Refocus generates a focal stack with video diffusion [ 58 ] , and AnyBokeh (not the video Any-to-Bokeh) edits photographs that already contain bokeh [ 19 ] . Conversely, EXIF-conditioned text-to-image generation uses the same AiF, depth, and lens-blur decomposition [ 55 ] . FlashReFocus likewise applies it to real photographs but replaces generative rendering with a lightweight feed-forward renderer that reuses the AiF image across edits.

Stage I adapts Stable Diffusion 2.1 [ 46 ] following PiSA-SR, starting from its released LoRAs, on two NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs with effective batch size 16, learning rate × 10 − 5 5\!\times\!10^{-5} , and 500 warm-up iterations. Synthetic pre-training uses three Hypersim epochs, batch size 4, and learning rate × 10 − 4 5\!\times\!10^{-4} . Five RealBokeh adaptation epochs follow, at × 10 − 4 5\!\times\!10^{-4} for the defocus-attention parameters and × 10 − 5 5\!\times\!10^{-5} for the rest of the network. Both stages use × 512 512\!\times\!512 crops, random scale, flip, and right-angle rotation. Runtime and memory are measured after warm-up. Metrics. For deblurring, we report PSNR, SSIM [ 66 ] , LPIPS [ 75 ] , DISTS [ 11 ] , the no-reference NIQE [ 35 ] , MUSIQ [ 23 ] , MANIQA [ 68 ] , BRISQUE [ 34 ] , and CLIPIQA [ 62 ] , and FID [ 16 ] . For bokeh rendering, we add MS-SSIM [ 65 ] , LPIPS with VGG features, CLIP-I [ 44 ] , and LVCorr [ 15 ] , the correlation between the strength setting and the rendered blur.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We presented FlashReFocus, an interactive refocusing framework that runs diffusion once per photograph rather than once per edit. One-step Stage I restores an all-in-focus image, and a lightweight renderer driven by an explicit defocus map then renders each edit in about half a second while leaving in-focus content unchanged. Beyond speed, FlashReFocus achieves the best perceptual bokeh fidelity on EBB! Val176 and on the unseen cameras of 3CReal, and its defocus map further enables aperture, tilt-shift, and two-plane control for practical, user-driven photo editing. Limitations. Blur follows monocular depth, so depth errors misplace it, and occluded background cannot be revealed. Distilling Stage I and video refocusing are future work.

sections.heading: B.1 Conditioning and Data Preparation
sections.text: Stage I follows PiSA-SR [ 57 ] on Stable Diffusion 2.1 [ 46 ] . At inference the U-Net runs at timestep 1 with an empty prompt and the VAE encoder uses its posterior mode, so an input always yields the same all-in-focus image, which every later edit reuses. Note that the detail weight ω \omega of Eq. 5 blends the two noise predictions rather than the LoRA weights: the detail LoRA is trained on top of the frozen pixel LoRA inside a nonlinear U-Net, so scaling its weights by ω \omega would not reproduce the blend, and ω ≠ 1 \omega\neq 1 takes two U-Net evaluations at the single timestep, a one-time cost per photograph. Within the network, LoRAs adapt the convolution, attention, and feed-forward projections of the U-Net and the convolution and attention layers of the VAE encoder. Training starts from the released PiSA-SR LoRAs: the rank-4 pixel LoRA is embedded exactly into the first ranks of the rank-16 one, and every rank keeps the released scaling. For distillation, CSD [ 72 ] uses the frozen model as teacher with guidance scale 7.5 and timesteps from 20 to 500. Its prompt is formed from the 50 highest-scoring RAM++ tags [ 21 ] of the sharp target, and its negative prompt adds bokeh, shallow depth of field, out of focus, and defocus blur to the official one; in addition, half of the training samples give the student an empty prompt. With ω ≠ 1 \omega\neq 1 , the adjustable mode of PiSA-SR computes ϵ pix \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\text{pix}} and ϵ pix+det \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\text{pix+det}} with two U-Net passes. Figure B.1 summarizes the mixed data sources: 350 training pairs of DPDD [ 1 ] , 4,179 filtered pairs of RealBokeh [ 50 ] , 11,261 training pairs of LFDOF [ 47 ] , and 639 sharp DIV2K [ 3 ] images for synthetic blur, 16,429 samples in total. Because many RealBokeh targets are not fully sharp, its scenes are ranked by the Laplacian variance of their small-aperture ( f / 22 f/22 ) images, and the top 1,000 scenes are kept. Likewise, DIV2K images with visible defocus are manually excluded, and the central 60% of each remaining image is used to generate synthetic pairs with Eq. 7 of the main paper. To make the synthetic blur less idealized, one kernel type per image is drawn uniformly from disk, Gaussian, and motion, which improves robustness to non-ideal real kernels; the image is then blurred at radii r k r_{k} of 1, 5.5, and 10 pixels, and the three results are blended per pixel with weights w k w_{k} derived from 𝐌 s \mathbf{M}_{s} , a ramp in one of eight directions (vertical, horizontal, and diagonal ramps in either sense, or radial from or toward the center, min–max normalized to [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] ) or a uniform map, drawn at random. Specifically, the weights are tent functions centred at c k ∈ { 0 , 0.5 , 1 } c_{k}\in\{0,0.5,1\} , w k ​ ( p ) ∝ max ⁡ ( 0 , 1 − 2 ​ | 𝐌 s ​ ( p ) − c k | ) w_{k}(p)\propto\max\big(0,\,1-2|\mathbf{M}_{s}(p)-c_{k}|\big) , normalized to sum to one, so the blur radius varies linearly along the ramp. sections.text: Figure 5 of the main paper isolates reconstruction errors introduced by VAE encoding and decoding; Figure B.2 shows the decoder guidance used to reduce these errors. Figure B.2 : Input-guided decoder refiner. (A) Multi-scale encoder features, each matched to the decoder block of the same resolution, (B) a high-frequency map, and (C) structure features of 𝐈 blur \mathbf{I}_{\text{blur}} are (D) fused into each block of the decoder, which decodes the Stage-I latent 𝐳 ^ \hat{\mathbf{z}} . The fusion modules and the decoder are trained with ℒ ref \mathcal{L}_{\text{ref}} while Stage I stays frozen. 𝐇 \mathbf{H} is contrast-enhanced for display. To locate the detail that the latent loses, the high-frequency input is computed with a single-level Laplacian pyramid: 𝐇 = | 𝐈 blur − G σ ∗ ↑ 2 ( ↓ 2 ( G σ ∗ 𝐈 blur ) ) | , \mathbf{H}=\left|\mathbf{I}_{\text{blur}}-G_{\sigma}*{\uparrow_{2}}\left(\downarrow_{2}\left(G_{\sigma}*\mathbf{I}_{\text{blur}}\right)\right)\right|, (B.1) where G σ G_{\sigma} is a 5 × 5 5\times 5 Gaussian kernel with σ = 1 \sigma=1 , ∗ * denotes convolution, ↓ 2 \downarrow_{2} keeps every second pixel, ↑ 2 \uparrow_{2} is bilinear upsampling, and the absolute value is averaged over the color channels. The degraded image and frequency map are then are concatenated and encoded as 𝐅 prior = ϕ prior ​ ( [ 𝐈 blur , 𝐇 ] ) , \mathbf{F}_{\text{prior}}=\phi_{\text{prior}}([\mathbf{I}_{\text{blur}},\mathbf{H}]), (B.2) where ϕ prior \phi_{\text{prior}} is a 3 × 3 3\times 3 convolution to 32 channels followed by two NAFNet blocks [ 10 ] , and 𝐅 prior \mathbf{F}_{\text{prior}} is bilinearly resized to each decoder stage. In addition, after every decoder up-block whose resolution matches a VAE-encoder feature of the input ( 𝐅 enc i \mathbf{F}^{i}_{\text{enc}} , from the input convolution and the first two down-blocks), a fusion module concatenates 𝐅 enc i \mathbf{F}^{i}_{\text{enc}} with the decoder feature, projects it back with a 3 × 3 3\times 3 convolution, appends 𝐅 prior \mathbf{F}_{\text{prior}} , applies two NAFNet blocks, and adds the result to the decoder feature through a zero-initialized 3 × 3 3\times 3 convolution, so the refiner starts as the plain decoder. sections.heading: Renderer topology.
sections.text: The renderer is deliberately small, with 1.30M parameters. Two 3 × 3 3\times 3 convolutions embed the mean-subtracted 𝐈 ^ AiF \hat{\mathbf{I}}_{\text{AiF}} , 𝐌 C \mathbf{M}_{C} , and a strength map into 16 channels, followed by a two-level U-shaped NAFNet: one NAFNet block per encoder level (16 and 32 channels, each followed by a stride-2 convolution that doubles the width), a bottleneck at 1 / 4 1/4 resolution, and two and four NAFNet blocks at the decoder levels (32 and 16 channels, pixel-shuffle upsampling, additive skips), and every NAFNet block reads 𝐌 C \mathbf{M}_{C} resized to its level. Attention is confined to the bottleneck, which projects its 64 channels to 96, fuses 𝐌 C \mathbf{M}_{C} , and applies three DRGs, each of three DAABs (three heads, MLP ratio 2, stochastic depth up to 0.1) followed by a 3 × 3 3\times 3 convolution over the features and 𝐌 C \mathbf{M}_{C} with a residual connection; the resulting 27 heads use the bias above with 𝐌 \mathbf{M} resized to the bottleneck. A last 3 × 3 3\times 3 convolution over the features and 𝐌 C \mathbf{M}_{C} predicts Δ ​ 𝐈 \Delta\mathbf{I} .

sections.heading: EBB! Val176.
sections.text: No evaluated method is trained on the EBB! training set, and because the official EBB! test set is not publicly available, we use its validation split. EBB! pairs are captured in the wild with a single Canon 7D DSLR and a 50 mm f/1.8 lens, the sharp image at f / 16 f/16 and the bokeh image at f / 1.8 f/1.8 , in automatic mode [ 22 ] . However, the two exposures are not aligned exactly: the authors register them with SIFT and RANSAC, crop them to their intersection, and downscale them to a height of 1024 pixels, so pairs may still contain viewpoint changes, exposure differences, black borders, and pixel misalignment. We detect mismatched pairs using SIFT feature matching [ 32 ] with RANSAC-based geometric verification [ 14 ] then remove visually invalid pairs, retaining 176 pairs ( EBB! Val176 ).

sections.heading: RealBokeh.
sections.text: We use the f / 22 f/22 to f / 2.0 f/2.0 pairs of 219 of the 220 validation scenes [ 50 ] at 2000 × 1500 2000\times 1500 (scene 200, a night shot of string lights with no in-focus structure to place a focal point on, is left out), with annotated focal points (Table G.1 ); the edit-consistency study (Appendix H ) uses f / 22 f/22 captures of the test split. Both are disjoint from the training pairs that adapt our renderer but share their camera and lens, so RealBokeh measures in-domain rather than cross-camera performance.

sections.heading: MODEST.
sections.text: MODEST [ 59 ] photographs each scene at several f-numbers. To evaluate a continuous range of apertures, from its camera-A 70 mm captures we pair an f / 22 f/22 input with f / 16 f/16 , f / 9 f/9 , f / 5 f/5 , and f / 2.8 f/2.8 targets of the same viewpoint, resized to a long side of 1536. We keep only aperture series whose targets are aligned with the input and show the same scene content, which gives 17 series from six scenes, and then place the focal point at the sharpest region of the f / 2.8 f/2.8 image.

sections.heading: In-the-wild images.
sections.text: Unsplash [ 60 ] photographs have no paired refocused references and are used only for qualitative comparisons, together with our own captures from an iPhone 15 and a Canon EOS 750D.

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: Baselines use released weights and official inference settings, except Swintormer [ 9 ] and Restormer, which are retrained on DPDD with their official code and settings. Unless otherwise specified, deblurring outputs are evaluated at the reference resolution.

sections.heading: Bokeh rendering.
sections.text: Focal points are manually annotated for EBB! Val176, 3CReal, and RealBokeh and shared across methods that support this input; auxiliary depth, disparity, or masks follow official inference settings. However, strength scales differ across methods, so each method renders a fixed set of its own strengths and the output with the highest SSIM to the target is evaluated. For instance, AnyBokeh [ 19 ] runs its official inference (Stage 1 on the whole image at 512 pixels, Stage 2 on overlapping 512-pixel tiles of the full-resolution image, 20 steps, guidance 30), and its strength is the bokeh scale of its optical fingerprint transfer, the ratio N src / N tgt N_{\text{src}}/N_{\text{tgt}} of input and target f-numbers. The scale starts at the EXIF ratio ( f / 16 f/16 to f / 1.8 f/1.8 on EBB!; per pair on 3CReal, and f / 16 f/16 to f / 2.0 f/2.0 for the eight X100VI pairs without EXIF) and is multiplied or divided by 2 1 / 4 2^{1/4} while SSIM improves. Tuning matters for this method: with the EXIF ratio alone, as in its paper, AnyBokeh reaches 22.27 dB PSNR and 0.2692 LPIPS on EBB! sections.heading: End-to-end refocusing.
sections.text: For the qualitative comparisons with the DiT-based DiffCamera [ 64 ] and GenRefocus [ 36 ] , the shorter side of every input is resized to 768 pixels with the aspect ratio kept, and all methods receive the same resized input. Since DiffCamera requires square inputs, rectangular images are reflection-padded to a square and the padding is removed after inference.

sections.heading: Efficiency.
sections.text: Cost is measured at 1536 × 1536 1536\times 1536 on one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPU under each method’s official inference settings, including patch- or tile-based inference where applicable. Parameters count every model a method loads, and FLOPs follow PyTorch’s FLOP counter (one multiply-add equals two FLOPs; element-wise operations excluded), and for diffusion-based methods, the cost covers denoising and VAE encoding and decoding. Deblurring time (Table 2) excludes disk I/O and is averaged over repeated runs after warm-up. In Table 6, in turn, New focus is each additional focal edit on the same image: FlashReFocus estimates the depth of the restored image once and reuses it, and its memory is the joint peak of both stages.

sections.heading: Metrics.
sections.text: We use PSNR, SSIM [ 66 ] , LPIPS [ 75 ] , and DISTS [ 11 ] for both stages. Bokeh rendering and refocusing additionally use MS-SSIM [ 65 ] , LPIPS with VGG features, and CLIP-I, the cosine similarity between CLIP ViT-L/14 [ 44 ] image embeddings of output and reference, following GenRefocus [ 36 ] . Beyond fidelity, blur-strength controllability is measured by LVCorr [ 15 ] with the protocol of GenRefocus [ 36 ] : for each all-in-focus image and a fixed focal point, using the 50 LFDOF [ 47 ] test scenes and the 89 3CReal inputs resized to a long side of 1024, a method renders ten strengths evenly spanning its own range, and LVCorr is the Pearson correlation between the strength and the rendered blur, measured as the negative Laplacian variance, averaged over scenes; for GenRefocus and AnyBokeh, whose ten renderings per scene each require full diffusion passes, we use the first 20 scenes of each set, on which FlashReFocus reaches 0.879 (LFDOF) and 0.792 (3CReal), against 0.690 and 0.666 for GenRefocus and 0.672 and 0.672 for AnyBokeh. Finally, no-reference quality is measured by NIQE [ 35 ] , MUSIQ [ 23 ] , MANIQA [ 68 ] , BRISQUE [ 34 ] , and CLIPIQA [ 62 ] for deblurring and by CLIPIQA, MUSIQ, and MANIQA for bokeh rendering; deblurring also reports FID [ 16 ] .

sections.heading: Implementation details.
sections.text: The framework is implemented in PyTorch and trained in half precision. Stage I uses a constant learning rate after warm-up; within it, the pixel phase optimizes the pixel LoRA, the VAE-encoder LoRA, and the U-Net input convolution, and the detail phase optimizes only the detail LoRA. In the subsequent refiner phase, Stage I is frozen, and the fusion modules and decoder of the refiner are updated in bf16 on 512 × 512 512\times 512 crops with batch size 4, learning rate 5 × 10 − 5 5\times 10^{-5} with cosine decay, 15K iterations, λ struct = 0.2 \lambda_{\text{struct}}=0.2 , and λ LPIPS ref = 0.1 \lambda^{\text{ref}}_{\text{LPIPS}}=0.1 . Renderer pre-training on Hypersim [ 45 ] and adaptation on RealBokeh use cosine decay and λ r = 1 \lambda_{r}=1 , λ LPIPS ren = 0.2 \lambda^{\text{ren}}_{\text{LPIPS}}=0.2 ; in both, the random scale factor is drawn from [ 0.4 , 1.0 ] [0.4,1.0] , flips are horizontal, and rotations are by a random multiple of 90 ∘ 90^{\circ} . At inference, the renderer estimates depth from the restored image with Depth Anything V2 [ 67 ] .

sections.heading: Depth source.
sections.text: The renderer is trained with Depth Anything V2 Large (DA-V2-L) depth, but it reads depth only through the normalized map 𝐃 \mathbf{D} , so any monocular estimator can be used at inference without retraining. To test this, Table G.4 renders the same inputs with the smaller DA-V2 models and with Depth Pro [ 8 ] , the depth estimator of GenRefocus, under the protocol of Table 3. sections.heading: Consistency across focal edits.
sections.text: Interactive refocusing moves the focal point many times on the same image, so each edit should change the blur and nothing else. We place eight focal points at depth quantiles from far to near over three 3CReal and three RealBokeh test inputs at a long side of 1024, and compare with GenRefocus [ 36 ] on two measures. In-focus fidelity is the PSNR and LPIPS between a result and the all-in-focus input over pixels whose depth lies within 0.04 of the focal depth. Edit consistency , in turn, is the PSNR between consecutive results over pixels whose defocus does not change between the two settings, i.e. whose distances to the two focal depths differ by less than 0.02. Both measures use the depth of our renderer. For a fair comparison, the two methods’ out-of-focus blur is equalized, measured as the mean absolute Laplacian over pixels more than 0.25 from the focal depth relative to the input, in two settings. In setting (i), GenRefocus runs at its default blur parameter K G = 15 K_{\text{G}}=15 and FlashReFocus’s strength K K is matched to it, per focal setting for fidelity and per scene for consistency; blur beyond the trained range is obtained by extrapolating the strength up to 2 or applying the renderer twice. Conversely, in setting (ii), FlashReFocus runs at its default strength K = 0.5 K=0.5 and K G K_{\text{G}} is set per scene to the same blur ( K G = 8.5 K_{\text{G}}=8.5 –14.19 on 3CReal and 5.25–7.69 on RealBokeh). In both settings FlashReFocus preserves in-focus regions far better (Table H.2 ): 44.44 dB against 28.96 dB on 3CReal in setting (i). This follows from the design: the residual renderer only adds blur to the restored image, whereas GenRefocus regenerates the whole image at every edit, so its in-focus regions drift from the input and pixels whose blur should not change still vary; between consecutive edits they change 2.7–3.7 times more than with FlashReFocus. sections.heading: Controls on a portrait.
sections.text: Figure H.10 applies the controls of FlashReFocus to one Unsplash portrait with three depth layers: the can raised towards the camera, the face, and the lake behind. All nine results reuse one restored image and depth, one renderer pass each. Moving the focal point blurs whichever layers are away from it, raising the strength with the focus on the face progressively blurs the can, and the depth edit of Appendix H keeps the can and the face sharp while the lake stays blurred.

sections.heading: Depth.
sections.text: The renderer reads the relative depth of a monocular model, so its errors become blur errors; a misestimated thin structure, glass surface, or reflection is blurred as if it lay at the wrong depth. Replacing DA-V2-L by Depth Pro or by smaller DA-V2 models changes PSNR by at most 0.11 dB on the benchmarks (Table G.4 ), but these averages do not bound the error on a single image with such content.

sections.heading: Occlusion.
sections.text: A real large aperture sees slightly around a foreground edge, so the background shows through its blurred rim. FlashReFocus, by contrast, renders from one restored image that contains no occluded content, so it can only spread visible colors and cannot recover the background hidden there.

sections.heading: Lens appearance.
sections.text: The renderer learns the blur of the lenses in its training data; it has no input for the aperture shape, which GenRefocus [ 36 ] can condition on, or for lens-specific effects such as cat-eye highlights. Moreover, strengths above 1 ( † in Fig. H.10 ) are extrapolated.

sections.heading: Restoration.
sections.text: Stage I can add texture that the input does not support or leave heavily blurred regions soft (Fig. F.3 ). In particular, when a face is strongly blurred in the input, FlashReFocus recovers it less sharply than generative refocusing methods, which synthesize new facial detail (Fig. H.5 , third row).

sections.heading: Cost.
sections.text: Restoration accounts for most of the 2.50 s first refocus at 1536 × 1536 1536\times 1536 (Table 6 ) and runs on a server-class GPU, whereas each further edit runs only the 1.3M-parameter renderer (0.47 s, 0.85 TFLOPs).

sections.heading: Video.
sections.text: FlashReFocus refocuses single images. Applied frame by frame, however, restoration and depth are estimated independently per frame, with no temporal constraint, so restored detail and blur can flicker; video refocusing needs temporally consistent restoration and depth, as targeted by video bokeh methods [ 71 ] .

sections.heading: Broader impact.
sections.text: Refocusing after capture can rescue photographs with a missed focus and gives casual photographers depth-of-field control without special optics. The restored detail, however, is partly generated by a diffusion prior, so a refocused image should not be treated as a record of what the camera captured, for example as evidence. The portraits in this appendix are Unsplash photographs used under the Unsplash License [ 60 ] .

Learn more × Back to arXiv License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.23297v1 [cs.CV] 16 Oct 2026 FlashReFocus: Interactive Image Refocusing in Seconds Ching-Heng Cheng Chia-Ming Lee Ming-Ching Chang Xin Li Yu-Lun Liu Chih-Chung Hsu † † thanks: Equal contribution. † † thanks: Corresponding author: chihchung@nycu.edu.tw National Cheng Kung University State University of New York at Albany National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University https://ming053l.github.io/FlashReFocus/ Abstract Single-image refocusing changes the focal plane and depth of field of a photograph after capture. It is inherently interactive: users try many focal points and blur strengths on one image, so each edit should be fast and change only the blur. Recent generative methods, however, rerun large diffusion models for every edit. We observe that the two sub-problems differ in kind: recovering the all-in-focus image is ill-posed and needs a generative prior, whereas rendering blur is largely determined by depth and the focal plane. We therefore propose FlashReFocus, which runs diffusion once per photograph and renders every edit with a lightweight network. To address the ill-posed restoration, a one-step diffusion deblurrer with a decoder refiner recovers fine detail efficiently while balancing fidelity and perceptual quality. For precise control, the renderer is conditioned on an explicit defocus map and uses defocus-bias attention, which lets pixels at similar defocus share information without interference from pixels at other depths; in-focus content stays unchanged, and editing the map yields tilt-shift and two focal planes. To further test generalization to unseen cameras, we collect 3CReal, a three-camera benchmark of 89 pairs. FlashReFocus achieves the best perceptual fidelity for zero-shot bokeh rendering on EBB! and 3CReal, refocuses 148.3 × 148.3\times faster than GenRefocus, and takes about half a second per further edit, 462 × 462\times faster. 1 Introduction Figure 1 : Refocusing paradigms. (a) Single-stage diffusion and (b) two-stage generative refocusing run a large diffusion model for every focal edit. (c) FlashReFocus restores the AiF image once and renders each new focal setting with a 1.3M-parameter network. (d) Seconds at 1536 × 1536 1536\times 1536 for deblurring, the first edit, each next edit, and both edits together. Figure 2 : Overview of FlashReFocus. (A) Stage I restores an all-in-focus image 𝐈 ^ AiF \hat{\mathbf{I}}_{\text{AiF}} in one step with a frozen latent diffusion U-Net and an optional decoder refiner; (B) ω \omega mixes the pixel and detail LoRA passes to trade fidelity for detail. (C) Stage II computes a defocus map from monocular depth and the selected focal point, and (D) renders bokeh in a single feed-forward pass with (E) defocus-bias attention, which focuses attention on tokens of similar defocus, more sharply for a larger strength K K . The bottom row shows the training phases. Depth of field determines which parts of a photograph appear sharp and is fixed at capture. Smartphone portrait modes move the focus afterwards only by blurring an already sharp image with depth recorded at capture [ 61 ] , so out-of-focus content stays blurred. Single-image refocusing lifts this limit by recovering an all-in-focus (AiF) image and re-rendering blur around a new focal plane [ 41 ] . Refocusing is interactive: a user tries several focal points and blur strengths on one photograph. Its two sub-problems differ in kind. Defocus is many-to-one: it discards high frequencies, so recovering the AiF image is ill-posed and needs a learned prior; regression-based restorers [ 25 , 73 ] over-smooth it [ 7 ] , whereas diffusion priors [ 18 , 46 ] synthesize realistic detail. In contrast, rendering blur is nearly well-posed: given depth and a focal plane, the circle of confusion (CoC) largely fixes the blur [ 41 ] , so generation adds cost and error rather than information. Recent methods nevertheless use large diffusion models for both. DiffCamera [ 64 ] and MagicBokeh [ 54 ] map the input directly to the refocused image and leave no reusable AiF image; GenRefocus [ 36 ] and AnyBokeh [ 19 ] split the task but render with a second large diffusion model. Either way, every edit is a full generative pass that takes minutes at 1536 × 1536 1536\times 1536 and regenerates regions meant to stay sharp (Fig. 1 ). This asymmetry suggests three principles for interactive refocusing, all followed by FlashReFocus (Fig. 2 ). (i) Generate once, render many. A session of N N edits costs C restore + N ​ C render C_{\text{restore}}+N\,C_{\text{render}} , so the generative step belongs outside the editing loop: Stage I restores the AiF image once with one-step diffusion [ 57 ] , and each edit runs only a 1.3M-parameter renderer. (ii) Edit only the blur. Changing the focus should leave in-focus content untouched, so Stage II adds a residual to the fixed AiF image; across edits, in-focus regions stay at 44.4 dB PSNR against 29.0 dB for GenRefocus. (iii) Control through optics. The renderer is conditioned on an explicit defocus map whose product with the strength mirrors the CoC, so the strength acts as an aperture and editing the map yields effects beyond a single lens, such as tilt-shift and two focal planes. Concretely, Stage I blends a pixel-fidelity and a detail LoRA with one weight ω \omega to trade fidelity for detail, learns from mixed real and synthetic blur, and adds a decoder refiner that keeps text and edges VAE decoding distorts; Stage II’s defocus-bias attention lets pixels at similar defocus share information, so blur changes sharply at depth boundaries without interference from unrelated, possibly salient pixels at other depths. The costly prior thus runs once, where detail must be invented, and each edit runs a small network on a task that optics constrain, which makes FlashReFocus both fast and accurate. Rendering also needs data with diverse focal settings: real pairs [ 22 , 50 ] capture lens-specific bokeh at few focal planes, and synthetic pairs [ 38 ] any focal plane with simplified optics, so we pre-train on synthetic multi-focal scenes and adapt to real pairs. Both are single-camera datasets, so we introduce 3CReal, 89 pairs from three unseen cameras, to test cross-camera generalization. Our contributions are: • For interactive refocusing, we propose a restore-once, render-many framework: diffusion runs once per photograph, and each edit runs only a lightweight renderer at interactive speed, leaving in-focus content unchanged. • To address the ill-posedness of defocus deblurring, we adapt one-step diffusion with a VAE-decoder refiner, which recovers detail efficiently while balancing fidelity and perceptual quality in a simple, unified design. • For precise control without complex designs, we craft the renderer’s defocus-bias attention and explicit defocus map, which set focus, strength, and depth edits directly. • To further test generalization to unseen cameras, we collect 3CReal; on it and EBB!, FlashReFocus leads in perceptual fidelity, far faster than generative rivals. 2 Related Work Figure 3 : Stage I deblurs in one step with separate fidelity and detail LoRAs. (A) A frozen U-Net with both LoRAs restores the input latent. (B) The pixel LoRA, a VAE-encoder LoRA, and the input convolution are trained with ℒ pixel \mathcal{L}_{\text{pixel}} and then frozen while the detail LoRA is trained with LPIPS and CSD. (C) At inference, ω \omega weights the detail branch and the refiner decodes 𝐈 ^ AiF \hat{\mathbf{I}}_{\text{AiF}} . Image restoration and defocus deblurring. Convolutional and Transformer restorers optimize reconstruction losses [ 10 , 30 , 73 ] and achieve high PSNR and SSIM, yet the perception–distortion trade-off [ 7 ] motivates generative priors for perceptual quality. Unlike motion or uniform blur, defocus blur has a point-spread function that varies with scene depth and focal distance [ 74 , 6 ] . Classical methods estimate a spatially varying kernel and deconvolve [ 26 , 79 , 76 ] , while learned models predict kernels or adaptive filters or exploit dual-pixel cues [ 56 , 42 , 25 , 1 , 2 ] , train on light-field pairs [ 48 ] , or model image formation explicitly [ 77 ] . More recently, diffusion models provide a learned prior over natural images for ill-posed inverse problems [ 18 , 46 ] . Restoration methods condition on the degraded image, predict residuals, or fuse latent priors [ 69 , 33 , 13 ] , and recent defocus methods combine diffusion with Transformer features or fidelity-aware guidance [ 29 , 9 , 27 , 28 ] . However, diffusion priors can hallucinate texture [ 4 ] and VAE compression loses fine structures; these issues motivate our detail LoRA and decoder refiner. Bokeh rendering and refocusing. Classical renderers convolve depth-dependent kernels, trace rays, or scatter in image space [ 41 , 24 , 40 , 70 ] , and layered or light-field inputs add scene information [ 61 , 37 ] . Learned renderers instead fit camera-specific appearance from data: they predict depth from one image [ 63 ] , learn DSLR blur from EBB! pairs [ 22 ] , refine analytical scattering [ 38 ] , render inpainted multiplane images [ 39 ] , add a strength control [ 50 ] , or model occlusion [ 52 ] . More recently, BokehDiff, MagicBokeh, and DiffCamera bring diffusion to bokeh synthesis [ 78 , 54 , 64 ] , including depth-free rendering [ 53 ] , and Any-to-Bokeh extends one-step diffusion bokeh to video with multiplane conditioning [ 71 ] , while Bokeh Diffusion controls the blur level of text-to-image generation but not the focal plane [ 15 ] . Across these methods, control signals range from scalar strength to masks, depth maps, and multiplane images; in contrast, ours is a depth-derived signed defocus map with a global strength. Refocusing further combines restoration with rendering. RefocusGAN estimates an AiF radiance image before applying focal blur [ 49 ] ; DC 2 uses a dual-camera rig [ 5 ] ; and GenRefocus trains two diffusion transformers, DeblurNet and BokehNet, for the two operations with semi-supervised learning [ 36 ] . Other methods avoid an explicit AiF image: Learning to Refocus generates a focal stack with video diffusion [ 58 ] , and AnyBokeh (not the video Any-to-Bokeh) edits photographs that already contain bokeh [ 19 ] . Conversely, EXIF-conditioned text-to-image generation uses the same AiF, depth, and lens-blur decomposition [ 55 ] . FlashReFocus likewise applies it to real photographs but replaces generative rendering with a lightweight feed-forward renderer that reuses the AiF image across edits. 3 Proposed Method Preliminaries. One-step Stage I restores an all-in-focus image, and a lightweight renderer driven by an explicit defocus map then renders each edit in about half a second while leaving in-focus content unchanged. Beyond speed, FlashReFocus achieves the best perceptual bokeh fidelity on EBB! Val176 and on the unseen cameras of 3CReal, and its defocus map further enables aperture, tilt-shift, and two-plane control for practical, user-driven photo editing. Limitations. Blur follows monocular depth, so depth errors misplace it, and occluded background cannot be revealed. Distilling Stage I and video refocusing are future work.
